title: Style and tone
note: Bathos is a fall from the lofty to the ridiculous; pathos is the quality that stirs pity. Litotes affirms by denying the opposite ("not bad"), while hyperbole exaggerates. A malapropism swaps in a similar-sounding wrong word, named for Mrs. Malaprop in Sheridan's 1775 play The Rivals; a solecism is any grammatical blunder.

items.a: elaborately ornate, of language or style
items.ex: His florid letters compared her eyes to twin moons over a sapphire sea.

items.a: pompous and overblown, of writing; also swollen
items.ex: Few readers got past the turgid first chapter of the memoir.

items.a: given to using long words
items.ex: The sesquipedalian professor never said "use" when "utilize" was available.

items.a: stiff and unnatural in manner or style
items.ex: The actors' stilted dialogue sounded like a phrasebook read aloud.

items.a: marked by an artificial or exaggerated style
items.ex: The director's mannered close-ups began to feel like a tic.

items.a: translucently clear, in meaning or style
items.ex: Her pellucid prose made a hard subject seem simple.

items.a: well chosen and apt, of a word or phrase
items.ex: Calling the tiny dog "Goliath" was a felicitous choice.

items.a: briefly and clearly expressed
items.ex: Give me a succinct answer: yes or no?

items.a: vigorously sharp and effective in expression
items.ex: Her trenchant review exposed every flaw in the plan.

items.a: biting and caustic, especially of humor
items.ex: The comic's mordant jokes about the tax code drew nervous laughter.

items.a: grimly mocking or cynical
items.ex: "Great, another meeting," she said with a sardonic smile.

items.a: sharp and harsh in tone
items.ex: The critic's acerbic column made restaurant owners dread Fridays.

items.a: dryly or mockingly humorous
items.ex: He gave a wry laugh at the parking ticket on his rental car.

items.a: amusing in an odd or dry way
items.ex: The guide's droll asides made the tax museum surprisingly fun.

items.a: playfully quaint or fanciful
items.ex: The café's whimsical decor included teacups hanging from the ceiling.

items.a: a sudden, ludicrous drop from the lofty to the trivial
d: a quality that stirs pity and sorrow
items.ex: "He gave his life for his country, and also his bicycle" is pure bathos.

items.a: deliberate exaggeration for effect
d: a mild word in place of a harsh one
a word used in place of a related one
items.ex: "I've told you a million times" is hyperbole.

items.a: understatement that affirms by denying the opposite
d: the misuse of a similar word
items.ex: Calling a marathon "no small feat" is litotes.

items.a: a mild word used in place of a harsh or blunt one
items.ex: "Between jobs" is a euphemism for unemployed.

items.a: the comic misuse of a similar-sounding word
d: a mild word for a harsh one
items.ex: "Dance the flamingo" for "dance the flamenco" is a malapropism.

items.a: a grammatical mistake or breach of etiquette
items.ex: "Between you and I" is a common solecism.

items.a: made stale and dull by overuse
items.ex: The ad leaned on the hackneyed line "It's not just a car, it's a lifestyle."

items.a: so lacking in originality as to be boring
items.ex: The interview stuck to banal questions about his favorite color.

items.a: a remark used too often to be interesting
d: a fall from lofty to trivial
items.ex: "Everything happens for a reason" is a platitude, not comfort.

items.a: a concise statement of a general truth
items.ex: "Knowledge is power" is an aphorism often credited to Francis Bacon.

items.a: a brief, clever, often witty saying or poem
items.ex: Wilde's epigram "I can resist everything except temptation" is still quoted.

items.a: the everyday language of ordinary people
items.ex: Dante wrote in the Italian vernacular rather than Latin.

items.a: a work imitating the style of another work or period
items.ex: The novel is a loving pastiche of 1930s detective fiction.

items.a: to mock publicly through satire
items.ex: The sketch lampooned the governor's habit of naming bridges after himself.

items.a: a figure using a part for the whole, or the whole for a part
d: a comparison using like or as
items.ex: "All hands on deck" uses "hands" for sailors, a synecdoche.

read.title: Notes in the Margin
text: Every editor has a private vocabulary of complaint, and a good one keeps it sharp. Here is what one veteran wrote in the margins of a first novel, and what each note meant.

Beside a paragraph comparing a sunset to "a bleeding tapestry of molten regret," she wrote "florid." Next to a love scene full of words like "pulchritudinous" and "concupiscence," she wrote "sesquipedalian; nobody talks like this." Where two characters exchanged lines that sounded translated from a manual, she wrote "stilted."
Some notes were praise. A single clean sentence about a father fixing a fence earned "pellucid," and an exact, surprising verb earned "felicitous." A widow's dry remark at a funeral got "wry, keep."
The harshest note came at the climax. The hero, having saved the town, wept for his fallen friend and then noticed he had lost a shoe. "Bathos," she wrote. "Unless you meant it, cut the shoe."

On the last page she left a summary that was both trenchant and kind: "Your instincts are good when you trust plain words. Every hackneyed phrase here is a place you stopped looking. Look again." The writer kept the manuscript for years, less for the corrections than for the lesson that style is a series of choices, and each one can be made deliberately.

q.q: Why did the editor write "Bathos" at the climax?
o: The scene fell from grief to the trivial lost shoe
The friend had not really died

q.q: The editor connects hackneyed phrases to
o: places where the writer stopped looking for the right words
